title: Mastering Spring MVC in Spring Boot

cards.title: Introduction to Spring MVC
cards.content:
Spring MVC (Model-View-Controller) is a robust framework built on the Servlet API that implements the classic Model-View-Controller design pattern.

  • Model: Encapsulates application data and business rules.
  • View: Renders the data to the user interface (Thymeleaf, HTML, JSP).
  • Controller: Processes requests, interacts with the model, and selects the view.

cards.title: The Front Controller & DispatcherServlet
cards.content:
At the heart of Spring MVC is the DispatcherServlet. It acts as the Front Controller pattern implementation.

Instead of mapping multiple servlets to different URLs, all incoming HTTP requests are funneled through a single DispatcherServlet, which coordinates the work required to fulfill them by delegating to specialized components.

content.instructions: Place the steps of a Spring MVC request in the correct sequence from start to finish:
items: The client sends an HTTP request which is received by the DispatcherServlet.
DispatcherServlet queries HandlerMapping to find the appropriate Controller.
DispatcherServlet executes the Controller handler method to obtain a ModelAndView object.
DispatcherServlet consults the ViewResolver to locate the physical view template.
The resolved view renders the model data and returns the HTTP response to the client.

cards.title: Creating Controllers in Spring MVC
cards.content:
Controllers are declared using the @Controller or @RestController annotations.

@Controller
public class WebController {
    @GetMapping("/home")
    public String home(Model model) {
        model.addAttribute("message", "Hello World!");
        return "index"; // returns the index.html template
    }
}

content.question: What is the primary difference between @Controller and @RestController?

options.text: @RestController is asynchronous by default, while @Controller is synchronous.
@RestController implicitly adds @ResponseBody to all handler methods, returning raw serialized data instead of rendering HTML views.
@Controller can only handle GET requests, whereas @RestController can handle all HTTP methods.
Only @Controller classes can be picked up by Spring Boot's component scanner.

cards.title: Handling HTTP Request Methods
cards.content:
Spring MVC provides shortcut annotations for mapping HTTP methods directly to your Java methods:

  • @GetMapping for HTTP GET requests (retrieving data).
  • @PostMapping for HTTP POST requests (creating data).
  • @PutMapping for HTTP PUT requests (updating data).
  • @DeleteMapping for HTTP DELETE requests (removing data).

cards.title: Path Variables vs Request Parameters
cards.content:
Spring MVC makes it easy to extract inputs from requests using mapping annotations:

// 1. Path Variable: part of the URL path structure
@GetMapping("/users/{id}")
public User getUser(@PathVariable Long id) { ... }

// 2. Request Parameter: query string trailing key-value pairs
@GetMapping("/search")
public List<User> searchUsers(@RequestParam String query) { ... }

cards.title: Working with Models and ViewResolvers
cards.content:
The Model acts as a map of key-value pairs passed directly to the view rendering engine. The ViewResolver acts as the translator.

For example, if a controller returns "about", Spring Boot's configured ViewResolver looks for a resource in src/main/resources/templates/about.html.

content.instructions: Match the core Spring MVC component with its primary responsibility:

pairs.value: Acts as the central front controller, dispatching incoming requests.
Identifies which controller method should process an incoming URI request.
Translates logical view names (like 'home') to physical templates.
A map-like container object holding data payload for frontend rendering.

cards.title: Global Exception Handling
cards.content:
Rather than managing try-catch blocks inside every handler method, Spring MVC offers dedicated global exception handling.

Using @ControllerAdvice (or @RestControllerAdvice), you can define standard fallback behavior for custom exceptions throughout your application.
